claims.text: Positive interactions, social support, and social connectedness on social networking sites were consistently related to lower levels of depression and anxiety.
Negative interactions and social comparisons on social networking sites were related to higher levels of depression and anxiety.
Of 30 studies examining total frequency or time spent on social networking sites, 8 found a direct positive association with depression and 16 found a nonsignificant association.
Of 30 studies examining social networking site use frequency, 3 found direct positive associations with anxiety and 7 found nonsignificant associations.
Applying Cochrane-adapted risk of bias criteria across two independent raters yielded a linear weighted kappa statistic of 0.78 (SE = 0.06).

evidence.description: Positive interactions, social support, and social connectedness on SNSs were consistently related to lower levels of depression and anxiety
whereas negative interaction and social comparisons on SNSs were related to higher levels of depression and anxiety.
Of the 30 studies examining these variables [...] 8 studies found a direct positive association with depression and 16 found a nonsignificant association.
For anxiety (and social anxiety), 3 studies found direct positive associations and 7 found nonsignificant associations.
A linear weighted kappa statistic for interrater reliability (.78, SE=.06) indicated that there was very good agreement in applying the bias criteria.

methodologies.name: Systematic Literature Review and Synthesis
methodologies.description: A multidatabase systematic search and qualitative synthesis of quantitative and mixed-method studies published between January 2005 and June 2016 examining relationships between social networking site use, depression, anxiety, and well-being.
conditions: English language publications between Jan 2005 and June 2016
Peer-reviewed journal articles or conference proceedings
Direct measurement of depression or anxiety in relation to SNS use
Cochrane-adapted risk of bias score below 3

limitations.text: Studies included in the review focused narrowly on young adult populations (late teens or early 20s).
The review search was restricted to English language, peer-reviewed journal and conference publications, excluding gray literature and qualitative research.
Methodology in the reviewed literature has predominantly focused on self-report cross-sectional approaches, which relies on participant retrospective estimates of SNS behavior.
Few studies in the reviewed literature considered individual differences such as gender and personality and their interaction with social networking site variables.

future_work.text: Leveraging real-time, unobtrusive SNS data over time through experience sampling methods (ESMs) and computational science techniques.
Expanding research across a broader demographic spectrum across the lifespan, particularly among older adults.
Investigating how individual user characteristics, such as gender and personality, interact with SNS variables to influence mental health outcomes.
